title: 95%-ile isn't that good
summary: Dan Luu: reaching the 95th percentile is not hard because almost nobody gets feedback; record yourself, fix basic mistakes, and the same applies to programming.

assertions.quote: most people can become (relatively) good at most things

verdicts.note: Consistent with deliberate-practice findings, but the game evidence is observational and self-selected.

assertions.quote: improve slowly when getting feedback would make improving quickly easy

verdicts.note: Coaching and feedback effects are robust in education research; the 'almost no one' part is anecdotal.
In the narrow domain of time prediction, structured feedback on one's own estimates (PSP, lessons-learned sessions) yielded no accuracy improvement, limiting the general claim.

assertions.quote: When I've recorded what people do and compare it to what they think they're doing, these are often quite different.

verdicts.note: Self-report of time use is known to be inaccurate; the twofold gain is a single self-estimate.

Observation logs revealed far more task and activity switches (13.3 and 47 per hour) than developers' stated concern about context switches would suggest, yet 8 of 11 still felt productive; tracking exposes behaviour self-perception misses, but the study finds much of it cheap rather than fixable waste.

assertions.quote: I now test each function as I write it to make sure they work
having a skilled coach or teacher give one-on-one instruction is more effective still

verdicts.note: Tutoring and expert coaching show large effects in education meta-analyses.

Review cites expertise research holding that deliberate training designed by a coach, not amount of experience, determines expertise, and that training improved estimation accuracy while experience had almost no effect; coaching is not compared with peer feedback directly.
